newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's Velayati gives green light for Total deal.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Velayati gives green light for Total deal.

text.p: Iran's foreign minister on Sunday said Iran had awarded French oil firm Total SA a $3.5 billion contract to lead the development of one of the world's single largest gas fields.
But comments by the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) and Paris-based Total indicated that a final document had not yet been signed and advanced negotiations were continuing.

A contract to develop Iran's offshore South Pars field would represent the single biggest investment in the Islamic republic since its 1979 revolution. It would fly directly in the face of U.S. trade sanctions imposed against Iran.

"Total has signed an agreement with the minister of oil of our country," Velayati said, speaking through a translator. "Total's contract amounts to $3.5 billion. It belongs to South Pars which is an important field for gas."

Industry analysts said Velayati's comments indicated that Iran had effectively given the green light to the French firm to develop the Gulf field after a series of detailed negotiations between NIOC and Total this year, but that the documents for signature had not been finalised.

Velayati was speaking in the context of Iran's ability to defeat U.S. sanctions. Under Washington's Iran-Libya sanctions bill signed by U.S. President Bill Clinton last year, the president has the power to impose sanctions on non-U.S. firms that invest $40 million or more a year in Iran's energy sector.
A NIOC official told Reuters that negotiations were still continuing with Total and also with a rival consortium led by the Anglo-Dutch Royal Dutch Shell Group.
"The foreign minister's statement is not correct as such. NIOC and the Ministry of Petroleum have not finalised any agreement with either Total or Shell," the official said.
"Our negotiations with the two sides are still continuing," the NIOC official added without elaborating.
Total also denied it had signed a contract with Iran, but repeated it was interested in the deal and talks were going on.
"No contract has been signed between Total and Iran for the development of South Pars, but the project does interest us," a Total spokesman said. "The negotiations are continuing."

Mahammad Nejadhosseinian, Deputy Minister for International Affairs at the Iranian Petroleum Ministry, said on May 10 at an energy conference in the Iranian city of Isfahan that the contract for South Pars would be announced within a month.

Total is already the leading foreign oil investor in Iran after scooping a ground-breaking $600 million in 1995 to develop Iran's Sirri E and A offshore gas fields, the latter of which goes into production next year.

It was not immediately clear how the Total consortium would be paid, but Iranian oil officials have said foreign contractors can get a return on their investment by taking a light form of oil known as "condensate" from South Pars as repayment.

Under the project, foreign participants would have no equity rights in the field and sovereignty of South Pars gas reserves -- conservatively estimated at 25.5 trillion cubic metres -- would remain firmly with Iran.

Total and Shell have led groups of European and Asian firms aiming to develop South Pars to produce 56.64 million cubic metres a day of gas after five years of project work. That gas would be the main source of supply for Iran's plans to export gas to Turkey and Pakistan at the turn at the decade.
Iran has the world's second largest gas reserves after Russia but exports dried up when it lost its main customer, the former Soviet Union, soon after 1979.

Velayati said the deal with Total, and the interest of European and American firms in an energy conference in the Iranian city of Isfahan earlier this month, showed that Washington's sanctions were having no impact on Iran.

"The managers of your oil companies are more clever than your people working in the (U.S.) foreign ministry," he said in response to a question from a U.S. reporter. "They know that if they don't take part...they will be behind European oil companies like Total, Elf, Agip and the others."
U.S. firms Mobil, Amoco and Conoco, part of DuPont, were reported to have attended the Isfahan conference despite the backdrop of the Iran sanctions bill.
The U.S. State Department is also investigating reports that NIOC has awarded a $140 million contract to a joint British- Canadian venture to develop its Balal oilfield.
